1:
Bede sets the errand in its practical frame: the devout women bought their spices once the sabbath was past and the liberty of working returned, but stayed away while night restrained them, so that coming very early shows their zeal and fervent love in seeking the Lord; he notes too that the first day from the sabbath is what Christians call the Lord's day, from the resurrection. Henry says they came to anoint the head and the wounded hands and feet and to scatter sweet spices, as we strew flowers about the graves of friends, only to show good-will. The hour raises the chapter's first difficulty, and the catena reports Ambrose owning that the place has perplexed many, since one evangelist puts the visit very early and another in the evening of the sabbath, with the suggestion that different parties of women and different appearances may be meant. A second discrepancy follows about how many messengers were seen. The catena preserves Augustine's reconciliation, that one angel was seen sitting within the outer enclosure and two others afterwards standing where the body had lain. Ellicott declines to harmonise and observes instead that at such moments of terror and astonishment perception and memory are not always definite.

On the angels' question Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic parable that turns on the same phrase reversed. A priest's foolish servant, hunting for his master, goes into the burial ground and calls out to ask whether anyone has seen him; being told that no one ever saw a priest among tombs, he is called a fool — and so, in the parable, Moses and Aaron say to Pharaoh that it is not the custom to seek the dead among the living, our God being the living God while the gods he speaks of are dead. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, him that liveth, and holds the question was enough to change the whole current of their thoughts, though he allows the words manifold applications beyond the primary one. Robertson notes what the appeal to memory implies, that they had utterly forgotten a prediction made plainly twice before, since it ran counter to all their ideas and hopes; Ellicott adds that the direct appeal to the women's memory is peculiar to this gospel and shows what does not lie on the surface elsewhere, that they too had heard the prophecies of the passion. On the messengers themselves Robertson observes that the text says men, not women, and that the dazzling apparel is described by a verb sharing the root of the word for lightning.

Cyril makes the sending a reversal: woman, once the minister of death, is now the first to receive and tell the awful mystery of the resurrection, so that the female race has obtained both deliverance from reproach and the withdrawal of the curse. The reception was otherwise. Ellicott notes that the Greek word for idle tales occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is applied strictly to the trifling babble of dotage; Robertson adds that medical writers used it of the wild talk of delirium, and that the verb for their disbelieving is imperfect, so they kept on distrusting. Gill collects the ancient versions, which give dream and jest for the same word. Clarke turns the linen clothes into an argument, that had the body been stolen all the wrappings would have gone with it, since stripping it would have cost delay and answered no end. Robertson twice flags the textual question, that this whole verse and several other phrases in the chapter belong to the shorter Western text bracketed as non-interpolations. Calvin thinks the order inverted, the running to the tomb having happened earlier, and reads the notice as sharpening the apostles' obstinacy, since Peter had already seen the empty grave when he still despised the women's report.
13:
Who the second traveller was is guessed at rather than known. Lightfoot has no doubt it was Peter, resting on a later verse of the chapter and on the apostle's list of appearances, and he identifies the speaker Cleopas with Alpheus, from the agreement of the name and from comparing three passages about the women at the cross, making him the elder of the two as father of four apostles. Clarke reports that many learned men ancient and modern took the other to be Luke himself, that some old versions actually insert the name Ammaus as though it were a person, and that the Persian version says positively it was Luke. Barnes reviews the same candidates and concludes there is no evidence to guide us. Henry rules Peter out on two grounds, that Peter was among the eleven to whom the two returned, and that anyone who knows Peter must think he would have been the speaker rather than Cleopas. Ellicott takes a different route, distinguishing the name from the similar one in the fourth gospel and deriving it as a Greek contraction indicating Hellenistic and probably Alexandrian antecedents, which may help explain why this man's story reached one evangelist and not the oral teaching behind the others.

On the village itself Barnes cites Josephus, who records that after the fall of Jerusalem Titus settled eight hundred discharged troops at an Emmaus sixty furlongs out, and canvasses a modern identification; Clarke gives the same distance and corrects the manuscripts that read a hundred and sixty furlongs; Ellicott notes that the name is probably significant, connected with the Arabic word for a bath and so marking warm springs, like the Latin and French names for spa towns. Why the two failed to recognise their companion is answered more sharply. Barnes says the expression means only that they did not know who he was, and that nothing supernatural need be supposed, since he appeared in another form and they were not expecting him; Clarke agrees and points to the same notice in Mark. Calvin insists on the opposite emphasis, that the evangelist says it expressly lest anyone think the features of the body were changed, so that the failure lay in the beholders and all suspicion of a phantom is removed. From that he draws a lesson about the senses generally, that eyes and ears discharge their office only so far as power is communicated to them from heaven, and that we should count it a daily favour that we see and hear at all.

Robertson finds a picture in the verb for their conversing, an old word meaning to throw back and forth like a ball, so that talk becomes a game of words; and he notes that the better text has them stop walking, the adjective for their faces being one that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Ellicott prefers that reading too, and says it has the merit of greater dramatic vividness; he renders the question literally as what words are these that ye bandy to and fro. Both he and Robertson correct the familiar rendering of the reply, which should be not art thou only a stranger but art thou alone a sojourner, Robertson glossing it as hast thou been dwelling all by thyself, since in Jerusalem everybody was talking about it. On the speech that follows, Barnes and Clarke independently make the same argument from its incoherence: Cleopas states things just as they occur to him, with little connection, his hopes and fears mixed into the narration, and this artless confusion is what a forger would never have thought to invent. Ellicott marks the emphatic pronoun in we trusted and reads the stage of faith exactly, that they believed him a prophet and hoped he would redeem Israel but had not risen to more.
25:
The rebuke is softened by nearly everyone who handles the word. Barnes points out that the term is not the one forbidden in the sermon on the mount, which implies contempt, but one denoting weakness or dulness, so that it was no expression of contempt but a charge of thoughtlessness. Ellicott says the same and adds that the word belongs to a somewhat higher style of language, being used by Paul of the foolish Galatians and by no other writer in the New Testament; Robertson glosses it literally as without sense, and slow of heart as dull, slow to comprehend or to act. Clarke turns the fault into evidence, that their very backwardness is a strong proof of the doctrine they afterwards believed, since men so hard to persuade would never have credited it without the fullest assurance, and they died on that evidence. Calvin refuses to soften it and enlarges the target: the reproof was not confined to these two but was meant to reach the rest through them, since Christ had so often forewarned them of his death and confirmed it from the prophets that he might as well have spoken to blocks and stones. On the exposition that follows, Clarke exclaims at the loss, wishing the discourse had been preserved.

That he made as though he would go further raises a question about candour, and three answers survive. Gregory takes the verb apart, observing that to feign means properly to form or put together, as a worker in clay is named from it, so that the Truth itself did nothing by deceit but exhibited himself in the body such as he already was in their minds. Augustine ignores the difficulty and reads the episode as a lesson in hospitality, that through this duty men may arrive at a knowledge of him, so that those who did not know him in the expounding of the Scriptures came to know him in the breaking of bread, since it is not hearers of the law but doers who are justified. Calvin meets the objection head on, granting that insincerity of any kind is a sort of falsehood and that the example has been used to license lying, and answering that the Son of God was under no obligation to make all his designs known, and pretended here in the same manner as he had given himself out to be a stranger on the road. Robertson notes the verb occurs only here, and Gregory draws the practical rule that strangers are to be not merely invited to hospitality but taken by force.

Whether the meal was the eucharist divides them four to one. Lightfoot calls it strange that anyone should expound the breaking of bread so, since Christ meant to disappear in the very distribution and the supper was over before it began, nor does it appear that any of them tasted a bit. Clarke says there is not the most distant evidence of it and calls it a mere family meal; Barnes agrees it was not sacramental but a common supper, and finds in it an example of seeking a blessing on daily food. Calvin reports that Augustine and most other commentators held the other view, allows it might be said with some plausibility that the Lord was recognised in the mirror of his own supper, but judges the conjecture to rest on no probable grounds. Ellicott takes the other side, holding the meal so full of spiritual significance that one may anticipate the technical language of theology and call it sacramental for them. A textual curiosity closes the scene: Lightfoot reports on the authority of Beza and Heinsius that a copy reads not was not our heart burning but was not our heart hidden, and Clarke finds the same in one manuscript and a Latin version reading blinded, though both prefer the burning.
36:
What the disciples took him for is worth pinning down, and Lightfoot supplies the categories. The Jews distinguished angels from spirits and demons, a rabbi defining spirits as those for whom souls are created without a body being made for them; but Lightfoot doubts the disciples meant anything so technical, and thinks they supposed this was not Christ in his own person newly raised but only a spectre in his shape, himself still dead. Clarke presses a doctrinal consequence out of the moment: if there were no such thing as a disembodied spirit, would the Lord not have corrected the error, whereas instead he confirms the category by saying that a spirit has not flesh and bones. Barnes reads the same implication, that the appeal presupposes a spirit may exist apart from the body. Calvin notes the awkwardness of the sequence, since only two verses earlier they had spoken of the resurrection as a matter fully ascertained, and now their senses are so struck that they think it a vision; he acquits them of fearing enchantments, and judges they were readier to believe an image of the resurrection was being shown them by the Spirit than that Christ was present. Robertson observes that both words for their fear are strong ones.

The proof offered is physical, and each of them presses a different edge of it. Robertson notes that the verb for handle is the one used in the first epistle of John as evidence of an actual human body, that flesh and bones tells against those who denied it, and yet cautions that we are not to conclude our own resurrection bodies will have flesh and bones, since Christ was in a transition state and not yet glorified. Ellicott holds the conditions must remain transcendental and mysterious, there being a real corporeity together with a manifest exemption from the ordinary conditions of corporeal existence, and points to the undesigned coincidence that what Thomas afterwards demanded was exactly the evidence he had heard was given here. Barnes lists the proofs plainly, that Christ showed hands and feet still pierced, told them to handle him, and ate before them, and that no better evidence could have been given. Calvin turns the verse into controversy: since the body may be touched and has solid dimensions, the passage refutes those who would have the body present where no mark of a body can be seen, for that would make it change its nature and cease to be what Christ here proves it is.

On their believing not for joy the reading is psychological and generous. Ellicott calls it characteristic of this evangelist to analyse in this way, noting that as men sleep for sorrow so they may disbelieve for gladness, the thing being too good to be true; Robertson says they were slowly reconvinced; Wesley grants they did believe in some sense, since otherwise they would not have rejoiced, but their excess of joy prevented a clear and rational belief; Calvin makes the joy itself arise from faith and yet hinder it, and draws the warning that we should regard the vehemence of our feelings with suspicion even when their beginnings are good. Robertson notes the best old documents omit the honeycomb, while Ellicott takes the two foods as evidence of ordinary diet and Barnes observes that the disciples gave what was ready. The catena preserves a reading from Gregory of Nyssa that the passover was eaten with bitter herbs while the bondage lasted and after the resurrection the food is sweetened with a honeycomb. Bede says he condescended not only to be touched but to eat, lest they suspect the appearance were imaginary. Calvin adds that he had no more need of food than angels, and dismisses as curiosity the questions whether it was digested.
44:
When this was said is disputed in passing. Calvin argues it belongs to the day after the resurrection, on the ground that what the fourth gospel reports of that day agrees with the words that immediately follow here; Wesley places it on the day of the ascension. On the threefold division of the canon the commentators turn cataloguers. Barnes assigns the law to the five books of Moses, the prophets to the former and latter groups, and the psalms to what was called the holy writings, listing the dozen books included; Clarke gives the same three heads with the Hebrew names, cites Josephus for a count of thirteen prophets and for the claim that the third division contains hymns and rules of conduct, calling that account imperfect; Ellicott notes that the last term stands for the whole of the Kethubim, of which the psalms were the most conspicuous portion. Lightfoot goes further afield and reports the rabbinic saying that wisdom has hewn out her seven pillars, meaning the seven books of the law, with the explanation that the book of Numbers is reckoned as three because two verses about the ark setting forward are counted a book by themselves. Wesley observes that little is said of the Messiah directly in the historical books.

That he opened their understanding is taken by all of them as the decisive act, and they differ on what it implies. Clarke says they had light enough before to discern the Scriptures as the word of God and as speaking of a Messiah, but not enough to apply them to their own Master, so that the book may be received as revelation while its proper reference is discerned only by the light of Christ; even the plain word, he adds, is a dead letter to the unenlightened. Calvin says the same in his own terms: the Lord had discharged the office of teacher with little improvement on their part and now begins to teach them inwardly by his Spirit, since words are wasted on the air until minds are enlightened, and the word is a lamp shining in darkness among the blind until the inward light is given. Wesley speaks of a veil taken off the heart. Barnes draws three lessons, that further truth removes present mysteries, that our own prejudices create many of them, and that only God can open the mind. Ellicott identifies the moment with the gift of the Spirit reported in the fourth gospel, and calls this evangelist's account vague because it came at second hand.

Two of them find the same force in the choice of city. Barnes calls Jerusalem the dwelling of his murderers and reads the order as showing his readiness to forgive the vilest sinners; Clarke puts it more sharply still, that the first overtures of mercy were made to those who had killed him, so that no sinner need despair. Calvin looks the other way, to the nations, holding that only now was it clearly discovered that the grace of redemption extends to all alike, since until the resurrection Christ was acknowledged as redeemer of the chosen people only, and that the priority given to Jerusalem preserves the covenant order. Gill separates the doctrine from its ground, insisting that repentance is no cause of pardon and makes no satisfaction, tears of repentance washing away no sin. Robertson notes a loose construction in the participle for beginning, and takes the promise of power as a garment put on, an old metaphor found in the poets. Ellicott traces the links forward, that witnesses is the key-note of the second volume and that the charge to wait in the city reappears at its opening; he observes the silence here about any return to Galilee. Calvin hears Christ claiming divine power by undertaking the Father's promise himself.
50:
Where the ascension happened sets off a small geographical crux, and Lightfoot lays it out in numbered difficulties. The same writer reports elsewhere that the disciples returned from Olivet, a sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem, whereas Bethany is put at fifteen furlongs, which is double that; and Josephus makes Olivet only five furlongs from the city while a sabbath day's journey is seven and a half. Lightfoot grants all three statements and reconciles them by distinguishing the town from the district that bore its name. Clarke reproduces the whole argument, numbered points and Josephus quotation together, and credits it openly to Lightfoot rather than presenting it as his own. Robertson simply places the spot on Olivet, near where the great discourse about the last things had been delivered, from which both Bethany and Jerusalem were in view. Henry reads the location as significant, since Bethany means the house of sorrow and there the agony in the garden had begun, so that those who would go to heaven must ascend from the house of suffering and go by agonies to their joys; he adds that Zechariah had long since named the mount of Olives as the place. Barnes recalls it as the favoured home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus.

Calvin makes the closing gesture an office rather than a courtesy. When men bless one another it is nothing but praying on a brother's behalf, but God does not merely befriend us by wishes, granting instead by a simple act of will what is good for us; and because he willed that men should have a familiar view of that grace, he appointed priests to bless in his name as mediators. Calvin traces the line from Melchizedek blessing Abraham, through the perpetual law laid down in Numbers, to the greeting in the psalm, and closes it with the apostle's rule that the lesser is blessed of the greater, so that the true and eternal priest must discharge in his own person what the law had enjoined on others. Barnes reads the same act more simply as commending the disciples to God's protection and guidance in the trials they were to meet. Ellicott raises the chronological difficulty here, admitting that this narrative taken by itself would leave the impression that the ascension followed within a day of the resurrection, and notes that the interval of forty days is stated plainly at the opening of the second volume; he suggests the devout women who informed this evangelist may have kept close within doors throughout it.

Two of the closing clauses are textually insecure, and both editors say so. Ellicott reports that the words about being carried up into heaven are wanting in some of the best manuscripts and are omitted by recent editors, and that the words about worshipping him are absent from most of the best; Robertson notes the same twice over, filing them among the shorter Western readings he has flagged all through the chapter, and remarks that the parting verb means he stood apart and was gone. Where the worship is retained, Barnes and Clarke build the same argument on it independently. Barnes observes that the homage was offered to an absent Saviour, after he had vanished from sight, so that it cannot have been civil respect but was the first religious homage paid to Jesus after he left the world, and that if worship may be rendered to him he is divine. Clarke puts it the same way, that acts of civil respect are always performed in the person's presence, so that they adored him as God. Calvin says the reverence was now paid not merely to a master or prophet but to the King of glory. Robertson ends on the joy, which he calls the note of victory.
